UX Case Study — 2026

PalUp

Finding your next meal companion —
one conversation at a time.

A mobile app that connects people for shared dining experiences in a new city, built from research through high-fidelity prototype.

Home

01 — The Problem

Moving to a new city means eating alone — a lot.

Communal dishes like hotpot and dim sum lose their appeal without company. Existing platforms like Meetup handle large events, but nothing exists for the simple, recurring need: finding one to three people to share a meal with. We set out to design a mobile app that makes it effortless to find a compatible dining companion — not just someone who likes the same cuisine, but someone you can actually talk to.

"People don't want a dining companion who likes the same food. They want someone they can actually talk to."

Core insight from user research

02 — Research

How we learned what users actually need

8 semi-structured interviews with Chinese immigrants living in Seattle (1–10 years in the US). Sessions were in-person and via Zoom. Participants lived alone or had limited social networks.

Key Findings

Theme 1

Conversation > Cuisine

Conversational fit was consistently prioritized over food preferences when evaluating potential companions.

Theme 2

Group Size Matters

4 people was cited as ideal — small enough to talk meaningfully, large enough to reduce awkward silences.

Theme 3

Safety Is a Prerequisite

Trust mechanisms were non-negotiable for female participants — safety was expected, not a bonus feature.

Theme 4

The Bad Cycle

Fewer friends → less dining out → harder to meet people. A self-reinforcing loop the app needed to break.

03 — Design Process

Four iterative phases

Each phase built directly on what we learned. Every design decision traced back to a specific finding from research or evaluation.

Phase 01

Paper Prototype

12 issues found

We sketched four core task flows. A cross-team heuristic evaluation surfaced 12 issues, three rated most severe:

Critical

  • →No send button visible in chat
  • →No way to leave a chatroom
  • →Event creation and home browsing shared the same screen

Before heuristic evaluation

Phase 02

Wireframes — Low Fidelity

Moved into Figma and connected all flows into an interactive prototype, applying every heuristic evaluation fix.

  • →Added floating "+" button as dedicated event creation trigger
  • →Added error states to the login flow
  • →Separated browsing and creating into distinct screens

Phase 03

Medium-Fidelity Prototype

Issue 1

Newly posted events weren't tappable on Home

Users had to navigate to My Events to see their new event.

Fix: All event cards made tappable across every screen.

Issue 2

"Vibe" field label confused participants

Options (Quiet / Casual / Deep) were too abstract to interpret.

Fix: Renamed to "Dining Atmosphere" with clearer options.

04 — Evaluation

What we tested and what we found

Two rounds of in-person user testing (heuristic evaluation + think-aloud sessions). 4–5 participants per round. No prior exposure to the prototype.

1

Round 1

Heuristic Evaluation + User Testing

Evaluated on the wireframe / medium-fidelity prototype using Nielsen's heuristics.

Task Issue Recommendation
Create an event After creating, event card on Home tab was not tappable — users had to navigate to My Events. Violates: Consistency and Standards. All event cards made tappable, linking to event detail page from any screen.
Create an event "Vibe" label and options (Quiet / Casual / Deep) too abstract. Violates: Match Between System and Real World. Renamed to "Dining Atmosphere"; options: Quiet Meal / Casual Hangout / Deep Conversation.
Find and join an event Participant avatars looked clickable but did nothing — users expected profile info on tap. Made avatars clickable to display participant profile details.
Find and join an event Keyboard did not appear automatically when tapping the search bar. Keyboard now appears immediately on search bar tap.
Communicate in chatroom Toggling "Mute Notifications" had no visible change. Violates: Visibility of System Status. Added pinned notice at top of chatroom showing key event info for all participants.
Login & manage profile Error message on failed login not visually prominent — easy to overlook. Violates: Visibility of System Status. Redesigned with stronger contrast and clearer placement.
2

Round 2

Heuristic Evaluation + User Testing

Evaluated on the high-fidelity prototype. Heuristic evaluation surfaced structural issues; think-aloud sessions with 4–5 new participants followed.

Heuristic Evaluation

Task Issue Recommendation
Cancel and Edit Event Users entering from Home had no way to cancel or edit — had to go to My Events. Limits flexibility of use. Added Cancel and Edit buttons directly on the event detail page regardless of entry point.
View Event details Only a small "›" button was tappable. Conflicts with proximity principle. Retained "›" as visual cue but expanded entire event card as the tappable area.
Communicate in chatroom — send message Chat input field positioned beneath keyboard, deviating from standard mobile patterns. Input field repositioned directly above keyboard.
Newly established chatroom — edge case No empty state design for a new chatroom with no messages or participants yet. Added empty chatroom state to represent real post-creation scenarios.
Login & manage profile Login & Security screen had no entry point for help or support. Added Help & Support button on the Login & Security page.

User Testing

Task Issue Recommendation
Create Event — preferences "Budget" ambiguous (total vs. per-person?). "Group Size" unclear if creator counted. Renamed to "Budget/Person"; added hint "incl. yourself" to Group Size.
Communicate in chatroom — report user Once a report reason was selected, users couldn't modify it without restarting. Users can now change selected reason before submission.
Communicate in chatroom — view user Could tap others' avatars but NOT "You" to view own profile — had to navigate away. Tapping "You" now opens own profile preview from within the chatroom.
Login & manage profile Confirmation screens lacked polish — hard to recognise completed actions. Redesigned with clearer card layout and subtle highlight background.
View Participants / User Profile Only part of participant list was clickable; avatars missing from list. Added avatars for all participants; made every participant clickable.

16

total issues surfaced across 2 evaluation rounds

Label clarity

most recurring friction — small wording changes had outsized impact on user confidence

Navigation consistency

users expected the same action regardless of which screen they entered from

Safety features

report flow and profile previews were expected even when not prompted

05 — Reflection

What we learned

What worked

A counterintuitive north star

Grounding every decision in one specific finding — conversational fit matters more than food preference — gave the team a shared reference. Every label and feature could be evaluated against it.

What we'd do differently

Broader pool, earlier metrics

Participants skewed toward Chinese international students. A more diverse sample would surface different safety concerns. We'd also introduce SUS and task completion rates earlier.

What's next

Matching, verification, empty states

A matching algorithm for conversational style. Verified profiles for safety. An empty-state experience for newly created events with no joiners yet.
